lesson.title: Same Object, or Just a Look-alike
lesson.summary: Object identity is about whether two names refer to the literal same object in memory, checked with is and id(), which is a fundamentally different question from whether two objects hold equal values.
lesson.body:
Every object that exists while a Python program runs has an identity: it occupies a specific place, and no other object shares that place while it exists. Python exposes this through the built-in id() function, which returns an integer that uniquely identifies an object for as long as that object is alive, and the is operator, which asks directly whether two names refer to that same object.

```python
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [1, 2, 3]
c = a

print(a == b)
print(a is b)
print(a is c)
print(id(a) == id(c))
```

This prints True, False, True, True in order. a == b is True because == checks whether the two lists hold equal values, and [1, 2, 3] equals [1, 2, 3] element by element. a is b is False, because even though a and b hold equal values, they are two separate list objects, built by two separate list literals, sitting at two separate places. a is c is True, because c = a did not build a new list, it just gave a second name to the exact same object a already refers to, so a and c are, quite literally, one object with two names. id(a) == id(c) confirms the same thing at the level id() and is are actually built on.

This distinction, identity versus equality, is not a technicality. It matters most with mutable objects, where changing the object through one name is visible through every other name that refers to the same object.

```python
c.append(4)
print(a)
```

This prints [1, 2, 3, 4], even though the code only ever mentions c, because a and c are is-equal, the same object, not just ==-equal look-alikes. If a and b had been treated the same way, mutating b would never affect a, since a is b is False: they are genuinely two different lists that only happen to currently hold equal values.

There is no dunder method for is. This is a deliberate design choice: == is a feature of a class, implemented through __eq__, and a class can define == to mean whatever makes sense for it, including something quite different from the identity check that == falls back to by default. But is always means the exact same thing for every object of every type: are these two names bound to the same object. That is precisely why is is the correct tool for checking against Python's singleton values, like x is None, rather than x == None: it asks the more fundamental, unoverridable question, which also happens to be a faster check for the interpreter to perform.

One caution belongs here, specifically because it trips people up. In CPython, the standard Python interpreter, small integers (from -5 to 256) and some short strings are cached and reused, so x = 5; y = 5; print(x is y) can print True, purely as an implementation detail of how CPython manages memory, not as a guarantee of the language itself. Relying on is to compare values, for integers, strings, or anything else, is a mistake waiting to surface as a bug the moment the numbers get larger or the interpreter's internals change. is is for asking "is this the same object," full stop, and == is for asking "do these hold the same value," which is almost always the question you actually mean to ask.
